channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Bittensor creator Const on Affine, dTAO, "mining reasoning," and more | E2326
gist: Bittensor founder Jacob Steeves, known as Const, explains how the Bittensor / Tao network extends Bitcoin's permissionless proof-of-work mining model to AI, using 128 competing 'subnets' (inference, compute, model-training) each with their own token priced against Tao via dTAO, while host Jason discloses a $500K-$750K personal bet on Tao and frames it, alongside Bitcoin, as one of only two crypto projects he's ever called 'definitely not a scam.'

insights.claim: Bittensor founder Jacob Steeves ('Const') says the project's origin idea was to connect the largest permissionless computer network in the world (the Bitcoin-style mining model) to the most important computational problem of the era, artificial intelligence.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Frames Bittensor's entire value proposition as literally 'Bitcoin's mining-market mechanism retargeted at AI compute/training' — a thesis investors can test against real subnet usage and revenue growth rather than narrative alone.

insights.claim: Const argues Bitcoin's core innovation was requiring token holders to 'make' new coins by solving a computationally expensive equation (SHA-256 hashing) rather than simply distributing tokens for free, which imposed a real cost (compute + electricity) to participate and created the first purely computationally-defined digital commodity.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: This 'cost-to-produce' mental model is the template Bittensor copies for every subnet's alpha token — useful for judging whether any new token design has real scarcity/production cost or is just free distribution.
insights.quote: You have to make them by solving this mathematical equation.

insights.claim: Const distinguishes peer-to-peer (direct transfer without an intermediary) from permissionless (anyone, anywhere, regardless of identity or intent, can contribute) as two separate properties Bitcoin pioneered together, and frames permissionlessness as a pure meritocracy blind to nationality, age, or regime type.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: This is the design principle Bittensor inherits for subnet participation: any bad actor can join, but the incentive architecture (not vetting) is what has to force good behavior — a key due-diligence lens for evaluating any subnet's security model.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says Bitcoin's hashrate/compute committed to the network has grown in an unbroken exponential line even while its price has been highly volatile due to speculation and shifting regulation (citing South Korea banning and re-allowing it as an example).
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Suggests miner/infrastructure commitment (hashrate) is a cleaner long-term conviction signal than spot price for permissionless networks — a lens that can be applied to Tao's own subnet compute growth as a leading indicator distinct from Tao's price.

insights.claim: Const calls Bitcoin 'probably the most efficient market we've ever seen in history' because anyone anywhere can buy, sell, or contribute hashing power to it with no gatekeeper, and separately states that Bitcoin is currently the largest supercomputer in the world.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Sets the scale benchmark Const is implicitly measuring Bittensor's AI-compute network against — Bitcoin's aggregate hash power is the one thing bigger than it, positioning Tao as the next attempt to build a comparably massive permissionless resource pool.
insights.quote: Bitcoin is probably the most efficient market we've ever seen in history.

insights.claim: Const frames Ethereum as having abstracted Bitcoin's immutable-ledger property into general-purpose smart contracts (citing MakerDAO-style collateralized lending/stablecoins as the payoff), while Bittensor is positioned as doing the analogous abstraction for Bitcoin's proof-of-work mining side — building a platform for many different 'mining networks' (subnets) rather than one fixed commodity.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Positions Bittensor as 'Ethereum for compute markets' rather than 'Ethereum for contracts' — a distinct category from most L1/L2 competitors, useful for sector-mapping when comparing Tao to other crypto infrastructure bets.

themes.theme: Tao Tokenomics & the dTAO Subnet Market

insights.claim: Tao has a hard cap of 21 million tokens, mirroring Bitcoin, with new Tao minted roughly every 12 seconds; the recent 'first halving' event has already cut that per-block issuance rate in half.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete, verifiable supply-schedule fact for modeling Tao's issuance/dilution curve versus Bitcoin's, including timing of the next halving.

insights.claim: There are currently 128 active subnets on Bittensor (up from an original single mechanism), with the team openly discussing expanding capacity toward 256 subnet slots.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: 128 is the current denominator for any 'how many subnets are actually good' due-diligence exercise; a move to 256 would roughly double the addressable slot supply and could pressure the price of registering a new subnet.

insights.claim: Registering a new subnet on Bittensor currently costs about 68 Tao (roughly $121,000) via a Dutch-auction mechanism where the entry price doubles every time a slot is claimed and then decays back down until the next buyer.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: This is effectively the 'seed round' cost of launching an AI/compute startup on Bittensor — comparable to a startup accelerator's investment size — and the team explicitly wants to lower it, which would change entry economics for new builders.
insights.quote: it costs about $121,000 to have one of these 128 slots which is a lot of too much and we want to lower that

insights.claim: Under the 'dynamic Tao' (dTAO) mechanism launched about a year before this interview, newly minted Tao is distributed to subnets based on the market price of each subnet's own 'alpha token,' effectively using an internal, permissionless trading market to rank and reward the ~128 competing subnets rather than a central committee.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: This is Bittensor's capital-allocation engine: Tao emissions flow toward whichever subnets the market prices highest, so tracking relative alpha-token prices across subnets is effectively tracking where the protocol's own 'venture capital' is flowing.

insights.claim: Each subnet has its own secondary 'alpha token' (also capped at 21 million units, unique to that subnet) that trades against Tao through an automated market maker (described as similar to a Uniswap V3-style pool) with slippage; users must first buy Tao before they can buy any subnet's alpha token.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Because every subnet token is paired against Tao, growth in any individual subnet's usage mechanically creates buy pressure on Tao itself — Const compares this to the US dollar benefiting from the network effect of every company operating inside the US economy.

insights.claim: Const states that when Bittensor increased ('tripled') the Tao emissions paid out to miners on a given subnet, that subnet's contributed compute capacity tripled within roughly two months, which he contrasts with traditional companies where deploying more capital requires hiring, contracts, and office space and does not scale nearly as fast or efficiently.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A concrete, testable claim about capital efficiency: permissionless incentive markets may convert new capital into supply/output faster than traditional firms — worth validating against on-chain subnet compute data before treating as proven.
insights.quote: But but a mechanism that's just just described by really just a code base and a permissionless market, you just pump more money through it and it just scales.

insights.claim: Const explicitly says a meaningful share of people who launch subnets are scammers, alongside credentialed researchers and self-taught entrepreneurs, because the permissionless registration process cannot filter for intent, only for measurable output.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A blunt admission from the founder himself that a nontrivial fraction of the 128 subnets are low-quality or bad-faith — reinforces that investors need subnet-level due diligence rather than assuming ecosystem-wide quality.
insights.quote: A good number of them are scammers.

themes.theme: Subnet Product-Market Fit: NG, Model Competitions, and Idle Capacity

insights.claim: The eny.ai / 'NG' inference subnet, run by ex-Google Brain researcher Ning Ren, offers inference for open-source models including Qwen (Qwen), Kimi (Kimi), and GLM52 (GLM-4.5) at roughly half the price of comparable centralized providers.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable price advantage (roughly 2x cheaper) is the clearest product-market-fit signal in the whole episode — investors can independently verify this by comparing eny.ai/NG pricing to OpenRouter or other inference marketplaces.
insights.quote: these tokens for Qwen Kimi and GLM52 are half the price of other places

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says he personally plugged the NG subnet's API key into his own agent tooling (his 'Hermes agent') after discovering the roughly 50% price advantage versus alternatives like OpenRouter, i.e., he is an actual paying user of a Bittensor subnet, not just an investor.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: First-person usage by a well-known tech operator is a stronger validation signal than any marketing claim — worth tracking whether other builders similarly adopt subnet inference for cost reasons.

insights.claim: Const explains that anyone with idle or unprovisioned server/GPU capacity (e.g., a rack awaiting a client for 100 days) can plug it into a Bittensor subnet like NG without asking permission and immediately start earning Tao, turning otherwise unmonetized downtime into revenue.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Positions Bittensor subnets as a liquidity market for stranded compute capacity — relevant to any data-center operator, GPU cloud, or hyperscaler customer with underutilized hardware looking for a yield outlet.

insights.claim: In a 'model competition' style subnet, Bittensor-trained miners produced a roughly 35-billion-parameter model that beat Qwen's (Qwen's) best model in that size class, but Qwen released an even better 35B model shortly after Bittensor's launch, illustrating how fast the competitive frontier moves.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence Bittensor's permissionless miners can briefly match frontier open-source labs at a given parameter scale, but also that any lead is likely to be transient — sets realistic expectations for how durable any single Bittensor model's edge will be.
insights.quote: Last year we did produce um a model that was better than Qwen's best model at the 35 billion range. And just before we launched it, they launched another 35 billion model that was better than ours.

insights.claim: Const identifies Liam, NG (eny.ai), and Affine as among the top-performing subnets on Bittensor, spanning GPU/compute aggregation, inference serving, and model-training competitions respectively.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A named shortlist of subnets the founder himself considers top-tier — a starting watchlist for anyone wanting to evaluate specific Bittensor subnets rather than the token as a whole.

insights.claim: Const says Bittensor subnets are designed so that even a maximally bad-faith participant ('if Hitler and the devil were to have a child') would be forced to produce genuine value, because validators judge miners purely on measurable output (e.g., does the server actually serve correct GLM52 inference) rather than on vetted identity or intent.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: This 'incentive-compatible even for bad actors' design principle is the core mechanism-design test for whether any subnet (or similar permissionless system) can actually be trusted at scale, independent of who participates.
insights.quote: if Hitler and the devil were to have a child when that child were to mine on your subnet they would just produce value

insights.claim: Const describes Bittensor's validator consensus as requiring more than 50% of validators (weighted by proof-of-stake, unlike Bitcoin's proof-of-work weighting) to agree on whether a miner's output is honest, directly modeled on Bitcoin's 51%-honest-majority security assumption.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Clarifies the actual attack-cost model for Bittensor subnets: an attacker needs to control >50% of stake-weighted validators on a specific subnet, not just outspend a single miner — relevant for assessing subnet-level security budgets.

insights.claim: Const says one of Bittensor's top subnets (referenced in conversation as 'subnet 51') solved GPU attestation without relying on hardware Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) like Intel's, instead building an algorithm that SSHes into a claimed GPU to verify it exists and is being used honestly, backed by economic derivatives to enforce it.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A concrete, non-obvious technical achievement (TEE-free hardware attestation) that could have applications well beyond Bittensor for anyone trying to verify remote GPU claims in decentralized compute markets.
insights.quote: trusted execution without trusted execution which is quite incredible. They don't even have tees

insights.claim: Inference-subnet verification uses a cheap cryptographic-style proof — in the case of the NG53 subnet, an algorithm called 'topology,' created by Prime Intellect, that hashes a model's intermediate hidden states and projects them into a different mathematical space to confirm a miner is really running the claimed model rather than a cheaper substitute.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Names a specific external technology provider (Prime Intellect) whose verification method is load-bearing infrastructure inside a live Bittensor subnet — a concrete cross-project dependency worth tracking.
insights.quote: they have to pair that result with a very cheap what's called a ZK proof

insights.claim: Const gives a concrete example of the fraud validators must catch: a miner claiming to serve GLM52 (GLM-4.5) inference while actually running a cheaper, lower-quality model like an old DeepSk (DeepSeek) build to cut compute costs while collecting full rewards.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Illustrates the exact economic incentive to cheat on inference subnets (substitute a cheaper model, keep the reward) that verification tooling like topology proofs must specifically defeat.

insights.claim: Const reframes inference verification as fundamentally an 'information checking/pairing' problem — proving the information a miner produced matches what a correct model would produce, as fast as possible — which he argues is the true underlying commodity being sold on an inference subnet, not 'inference' per se.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A reframing useful for valuing inference subnets: the product being priced is verified-correct, fast information delivery, so the real competitive moat is verification speed/cost, not raw compute.
insights.quote: inference verification is is actually information checking, information pairing.

themes.theme: Frontier Bet: Templar, Affine, and 'Mining Reasoning'

insights.claim: Const says decentralized training — many independent, geographically distributed computers jointly training a single large model by merging their weight updates each step — is the 'holy grail' of the field, harder than decentralized inference or decentralized compute aggregation, which is why the subnet pursuing it was named Templar.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Signals where Bittensor's technical roadmap is actually headed next (true decentralized frontier-scale training), distinct from the already-working inference/compute subnets — the harder, higher-payoff frontier to watch.

insights.claim: Const explains the core physical bottleneck for decentralized training: merging model weight updates across nodes requires moving on the order of a terabyte of data per training step, and a full training run of hundreds of thousands of steps would require communicating hundreds of thousands of terabytes — far beyond what home or laptop internet connections can handle today.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Quantifies exactly why training a frontier-scale (trillion-parameter-class) model in a fully decentralized way is currently infeasible on Bittensor — bandwidth, not compute or incentive design, is the binding constraint to watch for a breakthrough.
insights.quote: We're talking like a terabyte of data more, right? And if we want to do hundreds of thousands of steps, well, it's hundreds of thousands of terabytes that we need to communicate

insights.claim: Templar's decentralized-training work drew mainstream attention when Chimath Palihapitiya highlighted it to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on the All-In podcast, who reportedly called it impressive.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: External validation from a high-profile hardware-industry figure (Nvidia's CEO) is a notable credibility signal for Bittensor's decentralized-training research, worth checking against the actual All-In clip.

insights.claim: Const's current personal project is the Affine subnet, whose stated mission is 'mining reasoning' — paying miners to produce machine learning models optimized to generate useful chain-of-thought reasoning, rather than to be the best end-to-end model themselves.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Defines exactly what Affine is trying to commercialize — 'reasoning' as a separable, mineable commodity distinct from full-model quality — a narrower, more testable bet than 'decentralized AGI.'
insights.quote: reasoning is the way in which a model thinks to itself so that it can answer a question properly.

insights.claim: Const says Affine's mined reasoning models don't need to be stylistically perfect end products; at minimum they could function as 'adapters' that let a larger model like GLM think roughly 30 times faster by delegating reasoning to the smaller trained model.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A concrete, falsifiable performance claim (roughly 30x faster reasoning via adapter) that could be tested once Affine's outputs are integrated into a production model — worth tracking for a near-term proof point.
insights.quote: So you could run GLM and instead of GLM thinking you would just talk to the smaller model and then be able to go like 30 times faster.

insights.claim: Const states the long-term goal behind Affine is that mining/learning this 'latent space of thought' is a necessary prerequisite for eventually training frontier-quality models via Bittensor, not an end in itself.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Clarifies Affine's role in Bittensor's broader roadmap as a stepping stone toward competing with frontier labs on full model quality, not just a standalone product — sets expectations for a multi-stage bet rather than a near-term finished product.

insights.claim: Const frames the competitive stakes bluntly: 'we're up against nation states because this is truly like China versus the United States,' referring to the scale of capital and compute frontier AI labs and their backers can deploy versus Bittensor's decentralized swarm.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Sets realistic scale expectations: Bittensor's own founder frames the fight as nation-state-level, meaning near-term parity with frontier labs (OpenAI, Chinese labs) on full model quality is a long shot, not an assumption to price in soon.
insights.quote: It's not an understatement to say that we're up against nation states because it this is truly like China verse the United States.

insights.claim: The Templar subnet suffered a 'rug pull' when its team sold a large share of their tokens and left, then published a post blaming the network's leadership (calling Const an 'evil dictator') to justify their exit; Const says the project collapsed immediately afterward.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A concrete, named case study of subnet-level founder risk that critics use as an attack vector against Bittensor's architecture — worth weighing against the vesting norms that emerged in its aftermath (see next insight) before writing off subnet risk as solved.

insights.claim: Const argues rug pulls are structurally more damaging in crypto subnets than in traditional early-stage startups because subnet tokens trade on a live, liquid secondary market, letting a founder dump instantly, whereas illiquid private equity forces a founder to find a willing buyer first.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A double-edged-sword framework: the same liquidity that gives retail investors early access to Bittensor subnets (unlike accredited-investor-only startup equity) is also what makes rug pulls possible — a key risk/reward tradeoff to weigh before buying any individual subnet's alpha token.

insights.claim: In the wake of rug-pull incidents like Templar's, Const says many subnet teams have voluntarily begun locking their own alpha tokens for extended periods (some 'perpetually for years') as a public, on-chain signal of conviction to investors.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A checkable, on-chain due-diligence signal: investors can look at whether a subnet team has publicly locked/vested its own tokens as a proxy for long-term commitment before investing in that subnet's alpha token.
insights.quote: yeah, you know what? I'm locking this thing perpetually for years.

insights.claim: Const says that overall, across the Bittensor ecosystem, participants have made more money than they've lost, despite acknowledged rug pulls and scam subnets.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A founder self-assessment, not an independently audited figure — useful as a stated claim to weigh but should not be taken as verified aggregate ecosystem P&L without further data.
insights.quote: I would say that overall in the potential ecosystem we've made people a lot more money than they've lost.

insights.claim: Bittensor's governance is split between two entities: the original (Canada-based) Opentensor Foundation, now focused on marketing/outreach and no longer involved in development, and a newer, more insulated 'RA' foundation focused purely on core protocol development, which Const now works within exclusively; on-chain governance runs through a body called 'the triumvirate,' which is planned to expand into a more formal on-chain governance system this year.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: Maps the actual governance/control structure behind Tao — relevant for assessing decentralization claims and regulatory/legal exposure, since a formal on-chain governance expansion is explicitly planned for this year.
insights.quote: there's the open tensor foundation and there's the RA foundation and they they hold different sides.

insights.claim: Const states he believes Bittensor would continue functioning even if he personally left, pointing to the vibrant open-source community and the roughly 128 independent subnet teams that understand the technology as the network's resilience mechanism rather than any single founder.
insights.speaker: Jacob Steeves ('Const')
insights.so_what: A direct, testable claim about key-person risk — the bull case is that Bittensor's ~128-subnet ecosystem is decentralized enough to survive founder departure, in contrast to many crypto projects that collapse when the founder exits (as illustrated by Templar's own team departure).
insights.quote: I think it would definitely continue if I went away.

themes.theme: Jason Calacanis's Tao Position & Investing Playbook

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says he has personally called only two crypto projects 'definitely not a scam' in his lifetime: Bitcoin (where he says he made millions after buying under $100, though he separately notes he was hacked and lost some holdings) and Tao, on which he now predicts he will make 'tens of millions.'
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A rare, explicit high-conviction crypto call from a prominent venture investor — useful as a sentiment data point, though it should be weighed against his own admission of being currently down on the specific 2026 Tao purchase (see below).
insights.quote: I predict I'm going to make tens of millions. That's my goal.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis discloses he personally invested roughly $500,000 to $750,000 of his own money in Tao this year, describing it as a relatively small, non-fund personal bet, and says he currently may be down on that specific position.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete, disclosed position size and an admission of an unrealized loss as of this recording (Aug 2026) — gives a real data point on Tao's price trajectory since Jason's entry earlier in 2026, worth cross-checking against Tao's actual price chart.
insights.quote: let me put like I don't know if I put like half a million or 750 into this, something like that.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis publicly recommends that ordinary listeners simply 'buy one Tao' as a low-cost way to have exposure to and follow the experiment, explicitly framing it as speculative, not financial advice, and comparing the potential payoff to Bitcoin's move from roughly $200 to $60,000-$120,000.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A specific, low-commitment retail entry-point recommendation from a high-profile investor that could itself act as a demand catalyst for Tao among his audience — worth watching for any measurable price/volume reaction after this episode airs.
insights.quote: I think buying one tow just buy one tow is what I've been telling folks.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis describes his personal investing pattern-matching framework as looking for convergence signals — citing early Bitcoin true-believer energy (from a 2011 guest he didn't bet big enough on), the mobile+GPS+cloud convergence that produced Uber and Robinhood, and his early Tesla purchase — and says he now sees the same 'signaling' in Bittensor's passionate community.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A repeatable, named heuristic (convergence of technology trends + passionate early-adopter community = asymmetric bet worth sizing up) that investors can apply to evaluate other emerging categories the same way Jason applies it to Tao.
insights.quote: this reminds me of the mobile cloud computing era when like

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis explicitly distinguishes his approach from day trading, calling it 'J trading' — buying and planning to hold for a decade, while co-host Lon adds that the actual tactic is to wait for a bad news cycle to create a price dip, buy the discount, and hold long-term (both cite calling the bottom on Uber near $67 and buying Figma near $20, since risen to roughly $25).
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A stated, generalizable public-market entry tactic (buy the dip after bad news, hold for years) that is separate from the crypto/Tao discussion but reveals the same investor's broader risk approach, useful context for weighing his Tao conviction against his general track record and process.
insights.quote: I'm I'm not day trading. I'm J trading. J trading is hold for a decade.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis compares the risk of Bittensor subnet rug pulls and inactive/underdelivering Y Combinator-backed startups he's angel-invested in to a tolerable baseline fraud rate, analogous to the 1-2% fraud rate credit card companies accept as a cost of running an open payments system.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A useful risk-sizing mental model for any investor in permissionless/early-stage systems (crypto subnets or startup angel checks): expect a baseline loss rate from bad actors and size individual bets so that rate is survivable rather than assuming zero fraud.
